items: HTTP is stateless: every request independent, server remembers nothing
Cookie = small key-value string the server asks browser to store
Browser replays it on every later matching request
Sent automatically — no JavaScript involved anywhere
That automatic-ness is the root of CSRF
One `Set-Cookie` header per cookie — never comma-joined
All matching cookies ride in ONE `Cookie` header
`; ` separated: `Cookie: sid=abc; theme=dark`
Values must be URL-encoded before sending
Raw `;` `,` space or `=` in a value breaks parsing

blocks.title: Cookies Cost Bandwidth
blocks.text: They ride on EVERY matching request — images, CSS, fonts included. A 4KB cookie across 50 assets burns 200KB per page load.

blocks.title: Where To Put It
blocks.text: Cookie for anything the server needs. `localStorage` for client-only UI state. `sessionStorage` when it must die with the tab.

blocks.title: Not Encrypted By Default
items: Stored plaintext on disk or in an OS keystore
Profile folder access = cookie access
Sign or encrypt anything you actually trust
Session ID, auth token, CSRF token
Locale, theme, A/B test bucket
Analytics ID and consent record
`name=value` is the only required part
Everything after a `;` is an attribute
Order of attributes does not matter

blocks.title: Path Default Bites
blocks.text: `Path` defaults to the directory of the setting request, not `/`. A response from `/app/login` quietly gets `Path=/app`.

blocks.title: Session Cookie
items: No `Expires`, no `Max-Age` = dies on browser close
`Max-Age` beats `Expires` in all modern browsers
'Restore tabs' can resurrect a session cookie
`Secure` — only ever sent over HTTPS
`HttpOnly` — hidden from `document.cookie`
`SameSite` — cross-site send policy
`Partitioned` (CHIPS) — one jar per embedding site
Attributes are NOT sent back — only `name=value` pairs
Server cannot read a cookie's own `Path` or `Expires`
Unknown attributes ignored: `HttpOnley` fails with zero errors
Attribute names case-insensitive; cookie NAMES are not
`sid` and `SID` are two different cookies

blocks.title: Deleting Is Re-Setting
blocks.text: Same name, same `Domain`, same `Path`, plus `Max-Age=0`. Mismatch any of the three and you leave a zombie copy behind.

items: You cannot widen upward: `Domain=com` is rejected
You cannot jump: `app.example.com` cannot set `other.com`
No siblings: `a.example.com` cannot target `b.example.com`
Only the shared parent is reachable
Every rejection is silent — no error anywhere

blocks.title: Public Suffix List
items: Blocks cookies on registrable suffixes
`.com`, `.co.uk`, `github.io` are all off-limits
This is the 'supercookie' defence
XSS or takeover on `blog.example.com` reads a `Domain=` session
Worse: it can also overwrite that cookie
Cookie tossing: same name set on the parent shadows the real one
Shadowed cookie enables session fixation
Host-only is the safer default — widen only when forced

blocks.title: Port Is Not Scope
blocks.text: `example.com:3000` and `example.com:8080` share one jar. Two dev servers on one host will happily stomp each other's login.

items: Origin = scheme + host + port
Site = eTLD+1, the registrable domain
`https://a.example.com` vs `http://b.example.com:8080`
Different origins, same site — cookies see one thing

blocks.title: Scheme Is Half In
blocks.text: `Secure` cookies are HTTPS-only, but a non-`Secure` cookie set over HTTP is readable over HTTPS and vice versa. Cookies ignore same-origin policy.

items: Each tenant or app gets its own host-only cookie
Only SSO cookies deserve a parent `Domain`
Audit which subdomains you actually trust
Cookie path must be a prefix ending at a `/` boundary
Or exactly equal to the request path
Prefix-of-a-string alone is not enough
Default path = directory of the setting URL
Response from `/app/login` becomes `Path=/app`
Cookie then never reaches `/dashboard`
Always set `Path=/` on session cookies

blocks.title: Not A Security Boundary
blocks.text: Same-origin JavaScript reads cookies at any path through iframe tricks. Use `Path` for organisation, never for isolation.

items: Same name at different paths = two separate cookies
Browser sends both: `Cookie: sid=a; sid=b`
Send order: longer `Path` first
Equal paths tie-break by creation time, oldest first
Most servers read only the first — shadowing is trivial

blocks.title: Logged In As Someone Else
blocks.text: The server cannot tell which sent cookie came from which `Path`. This is a real source of wrong-user bugs, not a theoretical one.

items: Prefixes are enforced by the browser, not your server
The name itself is the contract
`__Host-` locks a cookie to the exact host
No subdomain can overwrite it — best anti-tossing defence
Use `__Host-session` for auth, always

blocks.q: When does a `Set-Cookie` update instead of duplicate?
a_bullets: Any difference creates a second cookie
That is how zombie sessions survive a logout

items: Browser sends the cookie only over HTTPS
`localhost` is exempted so dev still works
Without it, one plain HTTP request leaks the session ID
Hostile Wi-Fi plus sslstrip is a one-liner
It restricts SENDING, not writing

blocks.title: The Overwrite Hole
blocks.text: Pre-RFC6265bis, plain HTTP could overwrite a `Secure` cookie even without reading it. Modern browsers block that — older ones did not.

items: `document.cookie` can neither read nor write it
Does NOT stop XSS — stops token exfiltration
Attacker with XSS still rides the session via same-origin `fetch`
Still fully visible in DevTools and the network trace
It raises attacker cost, it is not a wall

blocks.title: So Pair It
blocks.text: `HttpOnly` only pays off alongside CSRF defence and short session lifetimes. Alone it just moves the attack from theft to riding.

items: Every auth cookie: `Secure` + `HttpOnly` + `SameSite` + `__Host-`
CSRF token cookie is the one standard exception
Double-submit needs JS to read it — deliberately non-`HttpOnly`
HSTS removes the first plaintext request entirely
Setting a cookie without `Secure` on an HTTP redirect page
Upgrading afterwards leaves the leaked copy behind
Conditional flags in dev config ship straight to prod
Use `https://localhost` with a self-signed cert instead

blocks.title: Verify In The Browser
items: No auth cookie without `Secure`
No auth cookie readable from JS
Check the browser, not the source code
`curl -i https://site/login | grep -i set-cookie`
Whether a cookie rides on CROSS-SITE requests
The browser-level CSRF mitigation
'Site' means eTLD+1, the registrable domain
`a.example.com` to `b.example.com` is same-site
Sent on link clicks and `window.location` navigations
Blocked on POST, iframe, `fetch`, `img`, XHR
Omitted attribute = `Lax` on modern Chrome, Firefox, Edge
Older browsers treated the omission as `None`

blocks.title: Strict's Real Cost
blocks.text: Click your app's link from Gmail or a search result and the first page renders logged OUT. Users read that as a broken login.

blocks.title: Browser Quirks
items: `None` without `Secure` = cookie rejected entirely
Chrome once gave new cookies a 2-minute POST grace window
Never build on that grace window
Safari/ITP blocked third-party cookies regardless — test it separately

left.title: Strict
items: banking-grade actions
admin panels
no smooth link entry

right.title: Lax
items: normal app sessions
default choice
links still work
`None`+`Secure` only for genuine third-party embeds
SSO iframes, payment widgets, embedded chat
Never as a shortcut to 'make it work'

blocks.title: Lax Still Allows GET
blocks.text: A GET that mutates state, like `/delete?id=5`, is CSRF-able even under `Lax`. Never mutate on GET — the attribute cannot save you.

items: Two-cookie pattern: `Lax` read session for smooth entry
Plus a `Strict` cookie required on state-changing routes
SameSite is defence in depth, not a CSRF replacement
Keep tokens for old browsers and same-site XSS

blocks.title: CHIPS / Partitioned
items: For third-party contexts only
One cookie jar per top-level site
The cookie cannot track across sites
Server verifies, creates a session record, returns an opaque ID
Cookie holds ONLY that random ID
User ID, roles, expiry all live server-side
Store is Redis, Postgres, or process memory
Each request: cookie, lookup, attach user, handle

lines: // >=128 bits, never a counter or UUIDv1

items: Logout is instant and real: delete the record
The ID becomes worthless everywhere at once
Ban a user, force-logout every device
Invalidate everything on password change
Revocation is the headline advantage
One store round trip on every single request
A shared store the moment you run two processes
In-memory stores plus sticky sessions break scaling
That is the classic 'random logouts after deploy'

blocks.title: Regenerate On Login
blocks.text: Session fixation: attacker plants an ID, victim logs in, attacker owns the session. Call `req.session.regenerate()` on login and on any privilege change.

items: Implement absolute AND idle, not one of them
Rolling without an absolute cap = sessions live forever
Set TTL at the store level or dead records accumulate

blocks.title: Fingerprint Softly
items: Store the session's IP and user-agent
Use them to flag obvious hijacking
Do not hard-bind — mobile IPs change constantly

blocks.title: Signed Cookie Sessions
blocks.text: Rails and Flask style: data lives IN the cookie under an HMAC. No store to run, but no revocation either, and the 4KB cap bites fast.

caption.text: Your session cookie is one missing attribute away from being someone else's. This field manual walks every `Set-Cookie` attribute, why `Path` silently eats your login, how a compromised subdomain can overwrite a cookie it should never touch, and where SameSite actually stops CSRF versus where it just looks like it does. Ends with the session-vs-JWT table and a ship checklist you can paste into your auth PR.
